deckTitle: Bullshit Jobs Uncut: A Field Report from Before the Timesheet

cards.power: Keeps the player alive for one more turn.
cards.lore: You bend, you gather, you repeat.
cards.gradeReason: Pure animal embodiment. No context needed. You already know this body.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Daumier ink wash. Subject: badger digging at dawn. Mood: primal exhaustion.

cards.power: Distributes action points based on natural stats.
cards.lore: The boy who won't sit still is sent out with the hounds.
cards.gradeReason: Lore lands if you know the story. Needs a beat of context at the table.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: watercolor pastoral. Subject: fox cub cast out from a den. Mood: matter-of-fact exile.

cards.power: Ends the turn when the resource pool is full.
cards.lore: No one tracks who did how much; the day ends when there is enough.
cards.gradeReason: Lovely concept, but pre-modern context means players need a moment to locate themselves.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: cave painting aesthetic. Subject: mice rolling a giant red berry together. Mood: communal ease.

cards.power: Detaches production from appetite, creating infinite output.
cards.lore: You no longer bend because you are hungry; you bend because you are the bender.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is one of the deck's best lines. You feel the trap close in real time.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ominous woodcut. Subject: beaver at a loom, food untouched beside them. Mood: haunted inevitability.

cards.power: Forces all units to pray in synchrony.
cards.lore: The day has owners, and the owners are calling.
cards.gradeReason: Power is a bit theologically odd; lore works but stays descriptive.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Hogarth engraving. Subject: monks and factory workers bowing to an enormous iron bell. Mood: obedient dread.

cards.power: Converts time from something you pass into currency you spend.
cards.lore: The factory's breath commands the herd.
cards.gradeReason: Visceral, immediate. The power text is a conceptual gut-punch all on its own.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: industrial watercolor. Subject: steam whistle blasting over stampeding cattle in factory gear. Mood: controlled panic.

cards.power: Treats daylight as the only legitimate constraint on availability.
cards.lore: Fourteen hours of the sun, all belonging to the mill.
cards.gradeReason: Solid but lore is factual rather than performative. Table-functional, not a showstopper.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Turner oil study. Subject: angry sun face setting over a textile mill. Mood: exhausted dominion.

cards.power: Reclaims 8 hours of what we will from the opponent.
cards.lore: The fiercest battle of the 19th century was over the right to go to sleep.
cards.gradeReason: The lore reframes the entire labor movement in one sentence. Absolute G1.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: protest broadsheet. Subject: raccoon in flat cap holding a banner reading '8-8-8'. Mood: furious hope.

cards.power: Breaks any job into terrifyingly efficient micro-motions.
cards.lore: He timed every breath until Schmidt moved 47 tons.
cards.gradeReason: Taylor's ghost made visceral. 'Every breath' is the detail that makes it horrifying.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Metropolis constructivism. Subject: weasel in lab coat pressing stopwatch to a tortoise's chest. Mood: clinical menace.

cards.power: Multiplies physical output by 400%; destroys the soul stat.
cards.lore: The first manual for treating flesh like gears.
cards.gradeReason: The 'soul stat' framing is perfect game-speak for something genuinely monstrous.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Bosch hybrid nightmare. Subject: pig-body mounted on tank treads, gears visible through skin. Mood: grotesque efficiency.

cards.power: Multiplies output by 240; removes the ability to craft.
cards.lore: No one here knows how to make a pin.
cards.gradeReason: Classic Adam Smith reference, clean execution. Slightly explanatory rather than performative.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Gillray caricature. Subject: bird, parrot, and mouse each holding one tiny piece of a pin, confused. Mood: fragmented pride.

cards.power: Prevents any worker from seeing the whole object.
cards.lore: The structural prerequisite for mass amnesia.
cards.gradeReason: Too abstract for immediate embodiment. Describes a condition rather than inviting a role.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: sectioned blueprint. Subject: disembodied hands each tightening a different bolt on a machine no one sees whole. Mood: eerie systematization.

cards.power: Extracts all value beyond the bare minimum required for survival.
cards.lore: The factory cannot function if the worker takes home what they make.
cards.gradeReason: Marx in card form. Correct and clear, slightly dry. Lore is explanation not invitation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: Victorian allegorical. Subject: walrus in top hat taking a pie from a cat waitress's tray. Mood: polite theft.

cards.power: The more wealth the worker produces, the poorer they become.
cards.lore: You build the world, but you do not live in it.
cards.gradeReason: Economical and devastating. The lore is six words that contain a century of critique.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: lonely expressionism. Subject: bear building skyscrapers reflected in puddle it cannot reach. Mood: magnificent exclusion.

cards.power: Traps all participants; leaving requires ceasing to be modern.
cards.lore: The Puritan wanted to work in a calling; we are forced to do so.
cards.gradeReason: Weber nailed but the lore is explanatory history rather than performance prompt.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: stained glass grotesque. Subject: bright bird pressed flat inside a Weber cage made of office partitions. Mood: rational imprisonment.

cards.power: Turns human activity inside a community into a commodity for sale.
cards.lore: In selling the hour, you sell the self that fills it.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is one of the deck's knockout lines. Immediate, personal, unsettling.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ink and blood wash. Subject: hourglass dripping red, a hand reaching in. Mood: intimate horror.

cards.power: Turns liberation into monolithic insanity.
cards.lore: Invented to give you room; used to fence you in.
cards.gradeReason: Good irony, slightly clunky power phrasing. The lore is the real payload.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: mid-century technical drawing. Subject: deer wandering between office partitions that form a maze. Mood: bewildered confinement.

cards.power: Cannot be coerced; must be manipulated and persuaded.
cards.lore: The worker owns the means of production—their mind.
cards.gradeReason: Drucker sharp. Power is punchy, lore is more aphorism than invitation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: propaganda poster. Subject: owl in suit at enormous desk, brain glowing behind glass head. Mood: self-important vulnerability.

cards.power: Replaces the factory whistle with ambient dread.
cards.lore: The soft power of the new regime.
cards.gradeReason: 'Ambient dread' is superb but the lore is too brief to embody — needs more bite.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: noir watercolor. Subject: avalanche of envelopes burying a duck at a desk. Mood: low-grade suffocation.

cards.power: Stops all actual work while simulating productivity.
cards.lore: The assembly bell of the white-collar world.
cards.gradeReason: Everyone knows this card in their bones. Universal G1, no explanation required.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: boardroom caricature. Subject: monkeys in suits at pie-chart presentation, one asleep. Mood: performative urgency.

cards.power: Work automatically expands to fill allotted time.
cards.lore: The project takes six weeks because six weeks were allotted.
cards.gradeReason: Parkinson's Law perfectly rendered but the lore restates the power rather than adding depth.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: comic strip. Subject: sloth surrounded by multiplying paper stacks growing to fill the room. Mood: comfortable bloat.

cards.power: Warps reality so the business only exists in three-month chunks.
cards.lore: The business shapes itself to what the analyst can see.
cards.gradeReason: Smart structural critique but more conceptual than embodiable for a casual player.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: teeth-and-eyes horror. Subject: carnivorous calendar devouring a long-term plan. Mood: quarterly bloodlust.

cards.power: Overtakes the real value it was meant to represent.
cards.lore: The system now serves the measurement of the system.
cards.gradeReason: Goodhart-adjacent, elegant but abstract. Works better as a lecture than a card role.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: shadow play. Subject: squirrels worshipping a cardboard sign labelled VALUE while real acorns rot. Mood: idol anxiety.

cards.power: Once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
cards.lore: Door-to-doctor time improved. The patient died.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is a perfect five-word horror story. Impossible to forget, immediately embodiable.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: clinical satire. Subject: dog on treadmill hitting dashboard targets while flatlining. Mood: triumphant failure.

cards.power: Tells a fiction about how decisions flow.
cards.lore: The real flows are sideways, informal, and invisible to the chartmakers.
cards.gradeReason: Astute but the lore describes rather than invites. Needs a player to inhabit to come alive.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: bureaucratic chaos. Subject: rooster at blackboard drawing flowchart while a yarn map behind shows something else entirely. Mood: confident wrongness.

cards.power: Scrambles the chart while ignoring the underlying flow.
cards.lore: A periodic ritual where everyone pretends things have changed.
cards.gradeReason: Immediately performable. Every table will have lived this. G1 on recognition alone.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: disaster vignette. Subject: Titanic deckchairs being rearranged by meerkats in suits. Mood: cheerful rearrangement of doom.

cards.power: Generates mutual dishonesty.
cards.lore: The place where the organization meets you once a year and pretends to know you.
cards.gradeReason: Two words of power, one sentence of devastation. This is precision engineering.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: uneasy portraiture. Subject: fox and dog across desk, both smiling too wide, papers between them. Mood: cordial theater.

cards.power: Pre-determines the value of units before they are even considered.
cards.lore: The line was drawn before anyone looked at your work.
cards.gradeReason: Stinging, personal, instantly recognizable. Every knowledge worker feels this in their chest.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: rigged courtroom. Subject: vultures in HR vests distributing value tokens before files are opened. Mood: preordained judgment.

cards.power: Allows the organization to claim it is doing something it isn't.
cards.lore: A person writes the report no one will read.
cards.gradeReason: Classic Graeber. Clear role but stays in description territory rather than invitation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: absurdist satire. Subject: parrot filling out forms with frantic intensity, stack disappearing into void. Mood: diligent futility.

cards.power: Exists solely to fix problems the platform refuses to repair.
cards.lore: Re-entering data the machine lost.
cards.gradeReason: Great Graeber reference but lore is a single example, not a guiding principle.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: frustrated realism. Subject: octopus with eight arms each holding a keyboard, re-entering lost data. Mood: heroic meaninglessness.

cards.power: Manages units that absolutely do not require management.
cards.lore: Creating busywork for the capable.
cards.gradeReason: Six words of lore that define an entire job category. Perfect performative clarity.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: absurdist hierarchy. Subject: hyena in hard hat directing competent beavers to dig a hole, then fill it. Mood: authority over nothing.

cards.power: Exists solely to make a superior feel important.
cards.lore: Feudal retinues in cubicle clothing.
cards.gradeReason: Four words that make you see the whole Middle Ages in every open-plan office. Knockout.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: heraldic parody. Subject: lion in Armani suit lounging while sparrows and mice arrange his aura. Mood: ambient deference.

cards.power: Exists entirely because the opponent has one too.
cards.lore: An arms race of useless aggression.
cards.gradeReason: Correct and dry. The concept is strong but the lore just restates the power.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: arms-race poster. Subject: two rhinos in suits glaring across a conference table, each holding identical dossiers. Mood: symmetric menace.

cards.power: Translates medieval guild progression into modern seniority.
cards.lore: The modern firm's imitation of the apprentice, journeyman, and master.
cards.gradeReason: Lore is a textbook definition. Neither invites nor provokes. Informative, not performative.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dusty woodcut. Subject: golden staircase ascending into fog, each step labeled with a corporate title. Mood: aspirational vertigo.

cards.power: The badge and the ceremony that bind the unit to the firm.
cards.lore: You ask them who they are, and they answer what they do.
cards.gradeReason: Strong lore but slightly scolding in tone rather than embodying. Needs table momentum.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: civic ceremony. Subject: peacock receiving a badge from a vending machine labeled TITLE DISPENSER. Mood: dignified absurdity.

cards.power: Exploits itself, removing the need for a boss.
cards.lore: The exploiter is at the same time the exploited.
cards.gradeReason: Byung-Chul Han distilled to one sentence. Lands like a mirror showing your own hand on your own throat.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: recursive nightmare. Subject: greyhound chasing itself on a treadmill, no handler in sight. Mood: self-propelled exhaustion.

cards.power: Triggers when the Achievement-Subject cannot stop being themselves.
cards.lore: You have no one to blame, because the only one pushing was you.
cards.gradeReason: Devastating callback to Card 36. The lore strips the player bare. Pure G1.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: tragic realism. Subject: smoldering pile of rubble wearing a tie, no villain in frame. Mood: self-inflicted ruin.

cards.power: Answers you in a way the spreadsheet never will.
cards.lore: Rediscovering work that pushes back.
cards.gradeReason: The concept is beautiful but 'pushes back' stays abstract. Needs a concrete example to fully activate.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: warm workshop light. Subject: raccoon reassembling a broken typewriter, tools spread across a wooden table. Mood: focused satisfaction.

cards.power: Remembers what to do when the mind has been trained out of it.
cards.lore: The whole object you can no longer build.
cards.gradeReason: Poetic and touching, but asks for a context to mourn — not immediately performable without it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: aged woodblock. Subject: gnarled hand holding a single dovetail joint, complete, no context around it. Mood: residual mastery.

cards.power: Cares about doing the work well for its own sake.
cards.lore: Cannot survive the modern firm's hatred of slowness and mastery.
cards.gradeReason: The lore explains its own tragedy instead of enacting it. Smart but one step removed from the body.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: sympathetic portraiture. Subject: badger carving wood, clock looming behind, colleagues glancing at their phones. Mood: dignified anachronism.

cards.power: Replaces deep mentorship with a PDF manual.
cards.lore: The apprentice no longer apprentices. The apprentice is onboarded.
cards.gradeReason: The lore's wordplay is clever but the card explains its irony rather than letting it detonate.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: corporate absurdist. Subject: puppy in VR headset wired to a drip labeled ONBOARDING. Mood: enthusiastic vacancy.

cards.power: Refuses to give the firm more than it pays for.
cards.lore: Labeled a crime by those who gave their souls for free.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is righteous and compact. Immediately takes a side and makes it defensible.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dry office comedy. Subject: cat sipping coffee beside a 5:01 clock, office fire behind, zero urgency. Mood: principled indifference.

cards.power: Do nothing, achieve nothing, want nothing the system wants you to want.
cards.lore: Only by lying flat can humans be the measure of all things.
cards.gradeReason: Radical philosophical position turned into a body posture. Immediately embodiable. The panda knows.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: manifesto poster. Subject: panda flat on floor, stock-market chart crashing behind, expression serene. Mood: horizontal resistance.

cards.power: The only place where work that matters happens at all.
cards.lore: Once a hobby; now a lifeboat.
cards.gradeReason: Punchy lore but it is wry commentary, not a role to embody.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: attic workshop. Subject: mouse painting a masterpiece at midnight, spreadsheets visible through the window. Mood: clandestine vitality.

cards.power: A 1930s prophecy that raises productivity but deletes free time.
cards.lore: We got the productivity. We didn't get the time.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is punchy but the power is explanatory framing. Both are too retrospective to fully embody.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ghost of prediction. Subject: dodo bird holding a Keynes pamphlet, surrounded by overflowing inboxes. Mood: hauntological irony.

cards.power: Work that does not begin, because it has not ended.
cards.lore: The structural unit of the new workday.
cards.gradeReason: Power text is conceptually tight but lore is a category label, not an invitation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: surveillance horror. Subject: enormous eye with Slack notification badge watching a sleeping figure. Mood: never-off dread.

cards.power: Pierces time zones, the kitchen, the train, and the toilet.
cards.lore: Someone needed to clear their queue before logging off.
cards.gradeReason: The power text is a geography of intrusion. Visceral, immediate, G1 by universal recognition.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: angry comedy. Subject: bear mid-bath, phone buzzing on the edge, message glow on wet fur. Mood: relentless interruption.

cards.power: Merges the bed and the desk into a single terrifying location.
cards.lore: A costume the office didn't know it was getting.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is perfect — deadpan, true, and funny in the exact right proportion. Universal post-2020 G1.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: uncomfortable domesticity. Subject: sheep in pyjamas and jacket top on a bed-desk hybrid, presenting to a screen. Mood: professional surrealism.

cards.power: Does not need a quarterly. Can wait forever.
cards.lore: Your job exists because no one has built a machine to do it yet.
cards.gradeReason: The lore is chilling but descriptive. Triggers dread without giving the player a role to inhabit.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: cold sci-fi. Subject: robot waiting patiently beside an empty desk chair, holding a clock showing infinity. Mood: patient displacement.

cards.power: Induces shame at our own slowness.
cards.lore: Surpassed by our own products.
cards.gradeReason: Too slight. Three words of lore on a concept that deserves much more weight. Underbuilt.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: melancholy still life. Subject: elderly tortoise watching a 3D printer produce a perfect tortoise shell faster. Mood: dignified obsolescence.

cards.power: A recovery period engineered to return you to work in better shape.
cards.lore: Leisure planned around work, ended by work.
cards.gradeReason: Tight and true but power and lore together stay explanatory — neither creates a character to play.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: vacation horror. Subject: pig on beach with umbrella drink, laptop open, clock in background. Mood: mandatory restoration.

cards.power: The activity that has no purpose outside itself.
cards.lore: The activity for which work freed you. We have very little left.
cards.gradeReason: The lore breaks the fourth wall in the best way. 'We have very little left' hits different after 51 cards.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: luminous pastoral. Subject: animals dancing in a clearing at dusk, no clock or building visible. Mood: pre-industrial wholeness.

cards.power: A quantity of human time and attention.
cards.lore: The day did not have to be filled.
cards.gradeReason: Quiet and profound but abstract — the player needs the whole deck behind them for the lore to land fully.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dawn landscape. Subject: rabbit holding a glowing sphere of light, nothing else in the frame. Mood: potential at rest.

cards.power: The answer to the day. The way things are.
cards.lore: After enough repetition, the other ways became unimaginable.
cards.gradeReason: Conceptually the strongest framing card, but its job is structural, not performative.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: industrial sublime. Subject: vast steam engine filling the horizon, tiny figures living their lives inside it. Mood: naturalized enormity.

cards.power: What you do because you are the kind of being you are.
cards.lore: The morning is easier when the Job and the Calling are the same.
cards.gradeReason: The power text is a definition worth tattooing. The lore is the test every player applies to themselves.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: stoic portraiture. Subject: lion waking at dawn with purpose, sunlight on fur, no alarm clock. Mood: autonomous readiness.

cards.power: The point of it all.
cards.lore: The system doesn't need us to know what it is for. But we need to know.
cards.gradeReason: Perfect closer. Shortest power text in the deck. The lore is both the question and the answer.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: threshold painting. Subject: FrizzleBob standing in open doorway, golden light outside, filing cabinets behind. Mood: earned departure.

verdict: This deck is a thoroughbred from the labor-history paddock — Graeber, Marx, Weber, Polanyi, Sennett, Keynes, and Byung-Chul Han all crammed into 56 cards structured by 14 Eras that read like chapter titles in the book you always meant to finish. Lore lines like 'In selling the hour, you sell the self that fills it' and 'The fiercest battle of the 19th century was over the right to go to sleep' land like gut-punches. The weakest stretch is Era 9 where The Ladder and The Goon feel thinner than their neighbors, and The Obsolete Man is the deck's only genuinely underbuilt card. The Era structure is the deck's flex move — it makes this the most teachable, most sequenceable entry in the What Work Was For trilogy. Table-ready: YES.
blurb: For workers, ex-workers, and everyone who ever stared at a timesheet and felt something die inside. 56 cards tracing the full history of work from the first bend to the final notification. Plays with your whole nervous system.

coverQA.coverVisual: 5 — FrizzleBob in industrial-office corridor, giant EXIT clock at 8:00, filing cabinets — tells the whole story in one image
coverQA.coverTitle: 5 — 'A Field Report from Before the Timesheet' is the best subtitle in the trilogy
coverQA.coverVibeMatch: 5 — exits, clocks, trapped animal: perfectly matches 56 cards of labor critique
coverQA.coverOriginality: 4 — strong but consistent with series aesthetic rather than breaking new visual ground
coverQA.coverViral: 4 — the EXIT clock is shareable; labor-history crowd recognizes the energy immediately
coverQA.coverNote: The strongest cover in the What Work Was For series. The EXIT clock at 8:00 is doing real rhetorical work — it's the factory bell, the Keynesian prophecy, and the escape hatch all in one. Could circulate in labor-adjacent Substack circles with zero additional context.

notes: 14 Eras function as named chapters — most structurally sophisticated deck in the series. Graeber's bullshit job taxonomy (Flunkies, Goons, Box-Tickers, Duct-Tapers, Taskmasters) appears explicitly in Era 8. The Achievement-Subject / The Burned pair in Eras 9-10 is a Byung-Chul Han two-card combo that works as standalone teaching material. Last page includes CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license notice and 'What Work Was For — v1.0'. G1 rate (43%) is above target but the lore quality across the deck earns it — no card has lazy writing, only varying levels of abstraction.

urgent: Punch up The Obsolete Man — three words of lore on a major concept is not enough; add a concrete example
The Ladder needs lore that makes a player want to BE on it, not just understand it historically
quickWins: The Goon: add a second lore sentence — 'An arms race of useless aggression' ends too early
The Division of Labour: 'structural prerequisite for mass amnesia' is brilliant but needs one grounding clause
niceToHave: Era 8 Graeber types (Flunky, Goon, Box-Ticker, Duct-Taper, Taskmaster) could anchor a standalone mini-deck booster
Consider a companion card for The Achievement-Subject showing what a non-exploited self looks like

marketingText:
Kayfabizarro: BULLSHIT JOBS UNCUT – A Field Report from Before the Timesheet (Free Cut & Play Comic Card Game)

What did your job actually produce today, before the part where you started looking busy?

Sit with the question, because the honest answer is the whole game. There is a whole class of work that exists only so someone upstairs can feel important, or so a box gets ticked, or so a problem nobody is allowed to fix stays quietly patched. Graeber gave the species their names. The Flunky, who makes a boss look bigger. The Goon, who exists because the other side hired one first. The Box-Ticker, who proves the thing happened without the thing happening. The Duct-Taper, who holds together what should have been rebuilt. The Taskmaster, who supervises work that was supervising itself fine. You already know which one signs your name to the timesheet. The opponent here is not your manager. It is the quiet agreement that a full calendar and a useful day are the same thing, and that the hours get paid either way.

Bullshit Jobs Uncut is Social Story Wrestling for the cubicle. Fifty-six cards trace the entire arc of work across fourteen eras, from the first task that simply ended when it was done to the notification that says the role has been made redundant. You do not study the critique from a safe chair. You clip on the lanyard and perform it out loud, and the table rules whether the job you just acted out is the one sitting in your inbox tomorrow morning.

WHAT'S INSIDE?
- The Bullshit Jobs Core Deck: 56 High-Res "Print, Cut & Play" Cards across fourteen eras, featuring The Flunky (the role that exists purely so somebody else looks more important), The Goodhart Metric (the number that stopped measuring the work the second it became the target), and Lying Flat (Tang Ping) (the worker who quit the race by simply, gloriously, doing less).
- The Freestyle Rules: The complete Anti-Rulebook. No spreadsheets, no math, just storytelling, dice-driven chaos, and the Blödsinn! call for anyone who defends a job by listing how full their week is.
- The Fourteen Eras: every chapter a stage in how busywork got invented and then sold back to you, so the full deck reads as a field report on a trap that pays you to keep maintaining it.

THE "LIVING DECK" PASS (Free Updates)
This deck runs the same series as What Work Was For, so grabbing it puts you in the line. Every future chapter and expansion in the work cycle arrives in your library as a free update. The clock keeps adding shifts. So does the deck.

WHY "PAY WHAT YOU WANT"?
I make these because somebody convinced an entire planet that looking busy is the same as being worth something, and the counter-story should cost less than the lie did. Broke, between jobs, or already handing enough hours to a role that hands nothing back? Enter "0" and take it. Print it, cut it, deal it in the break room. Want to support the craft? Every dollar goes straight into drawing the next cards. Free to share and adapt under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Never resell.

Choose your reality. Become an Epistemic Outlaw.
Half the job was always pretending the job mattered. Put that mask on the desk and deal the honest one.
Stay fluffy. — Uncle FrizzleBob
